body_markdown:
A localized outbreak of flea borne typhus in Los Angeles has prompted health officials to remind residents about the importance of flea control, pet protection and measures to keep rodents and wildlife away from homes.


The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health said seven people were identified as having symptomatic flea borne typhus linked to an outbreak in the Wilshire Center neighborhood. Six of those patients required hospitalization. Health officials said all seven people have since recovered.


The outbreak is the second cluster of flea borne typhus reported by Los Angeles County health authorities this year. The development comes as officials continue monitoring an increase in reported cases across the county.


## What Is Flea Borne Typhus?


Flea borne typhus, also known as murine typhus or endemic typhus, is a bacterial infection caused by *Rickettsia typhi* . Unlike some other forms of typhus, it is associated with infected fleas rather than person to person transmission.


According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, people can become infected when they come into contact with infected flea feces. The bacteria can enter the body through scratches, cuts or other breaks in the skin. Exposure can also occur if contaminated flea dirt comes into contact with the eyes or is inhaled.


Fleas can become infected after feeding on animals carrying the bacteria. Rats, opossums and cats can play a role in maintaining flea populations in urban and suburban environments. Pets that spend time outdoors can also carry fleas into areas where people live.


Importantly, flea borne typhus does not normally spread directly from one person to another.


## Los Angeles Sees Continued Flea Borne Typhus Activity


The latest Los Angeles outbreak highlights an ongoing public health concern in parts of Southern California.


The county health department reported 109 flea borne typhus cases so far in 2026. In 2025, Los Angeles County recorded 220 cases, compared with 187 cases in 2024, according to the information provided by county health officials.


Public health officials say cases can occur throughout the year, although activity generally increases during late summer and fall.


The recent outbreaks have particularly affected areas of Central and South Los Angeles.


Los Angeles County Health Officer Muntu Davis urged residents to take steps to reduce exposure to fleas, particularly those carried by free roaming animals and wildlife.


Health officials have emphasized that simple household and pet care measures can reduce the opportunity for infected fleas to come into contact with people.


## Symptoms of Flea Borne Typhus


Flea borne typhus can initially resemble several other illnesses, which can make it difficult to recognize based on symptoms alone.


The CDC says symptoms commonly develop within several days to two weeks after exposure. Common symptoms include:


- Fever
- Chills
- Headache
- Muscle and body aches
- Loss of appetite
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Stomach pain
- Cough
- Skin rash


A rash can occur, but not everyone develops one. The CDC notes that the rash typically appears toward the end of the first week of illness and may begin on the torso before spreading.


Because the symptoms can overlap with other infections, people may not immediately realize that fleas or flea contaminated material were involved.


The CDC also notes that many people do not remember being bitten by a flea before becoming sick. This means the absence of a known flea bite does not necessarily rule out flea borne typhus.


## Can Flea Borne Typhus Become Serious?


Many people recover when the infection is recognized and treated promptly. However, severe illness can occur, and some patients may require hospitalization.


The recent Los Angeles outbreak illustrates that hospitalization can occur even though the infection is treatable.


According to the CDC, untreated flea borne typhus can lead to more serious illness, including organ complications. Death is uncommon, but severe and fatal cases have been documented.


Early medical attention is therefore important when someone develops compatible symptoms, particularly when there has been possible exposure to fleas, rodents, stray animals or wildlife.


## Why Early Treatment Matters


Flea borne typhus is generally treated with the antibiotic doxycycline. CDC guidance says treatment should be considered based on clinical suspicion and should not necessarily be delayed while waiting for laboratory confirmation.


Early treatment can shorten the illness and reduce the likelihood of severe complications.


Laboratory testing can be challenging because some diagnostic tests may not provide definitive results during the earliest stages of infection. Healthcare professionals therefore consider symptoms, exposure history and other clinical information when deciding whether treatment is appropriate.


Anyone experiencing persistent fever or other concerning symptoms should speak with a healthcare professional rather than attempting to diagnose or treat the illness independently.


## How Residents Can Reduce the Risk


There is currently no vaccine available to prevent flea borne typhus. Prevention focuses largely on reducing contact with infected fleas and controlling the animals that can carry them.


Health authorities recommend several practical steps.


### Protect Pets From Fleas


Dogs and cats that spend time outdoors can pick up fleas and bring them into homes.


Pet owners should discuss year round flea prevention with a veterinarian and use products appropriate for their animals. Keeping pets indoors when practical can also reduce their exposure to fleas.


### Keep Rodents and Wildlife Away


Residents should remove conditions that attract rats and other wildlife.


This can include:


- Keeping garbage containers securely closed
- Storing food and pet food in sealed containers
- Removing outdoor clutter and debris
- Clearing brush and overgrown vegetation
- Sealing openings where rodents could enter buildings
- Avoiding outdoor food sources that can attract animals


The CDC specifically recommends reducing access to food, removing potential animal shelters and sealing gaps that could allow rodents to enter buildings.


### Avoid Contact With Stray and Wild Animals


People should avoid feeding or handling wild animals and stray animals whenever possible.


Opossums, rats and free roaming cats can be associated with fleas capable of transmitting *Rickettsia typhi* . Residents who regularly encounter stray animals around their property can contact local animal control or appropriate community services rather than attempting to handle the animals themselves.


### Take Precautions Outdoors


People spending time outdoors in areas where fleas may be present can use an EPA registered insect repellent according to the product label.


The CDC also recommends taking steps to avoid flea exposure and maintaining appropriate flea prevention for household pets.


## What the Los Angeles Outbreak Means for Residents


The latest outbreak does not mean that everyone in Los Angeles is at high risk of developing flea borne typhus. Instead, the situation serves as a reminder that the disease remains present in some communities and that exposure can occur around homes, pets and areas where rodents or wildlife are active.


The fact that all seven people linked to the latest reported cluster have recovered is also important context. Flea borne typhus is treatable, particularly when medical care is obtained promptly.


Residents who develop unexplained fever, headache, body aches, nausea, vomiting or rash should contact a healthcare professional. People should mention any known or possible exposure to fleas, outdoor animals, rodents, stray cats or wildlife because that information may help clinicians consider flea borne typhus among possible causes.


## Final Takeaway


The flea borne typhus outbreak reported in Los Angeles has renewed attention on a disease that can be transmitted through infected fleas and flea contaminated material.


Seven people were linked to the latest Wilshire Center outbreak, with six requiring hospitalization. All seven have recovered, according to Los Angeles County health officials.


For residents, prevention largely comes down to controlling fleas, protecting pets, reducing rodent and wildlife activity around homes and seeking medical attention when concerning symptoms develop.


With no vaccine currently available, awareness and prevention remain important tools for reducing exposure.
